newsitem.title: CHINA: China's television king expects to stay ahead.
newsitem.headline: China's television king expects to stay ahead.

text.p: China's colour television king, Sichuan Changhong Electric Co (Group), has few regrets about sparking a price war in 1996 and expects to remain on top despite stiff competition, officials said.

Changhong, whose subsidiary Sichuan Changhong Electric Co lists domestic currency A shares in Shanghai, started the price war last March, shaking smaller producers out of the industry and hurting profits at all companies.
"Price cutting is one method of competing in the market economy," Yu Guangyin, vice-chairman of the board of Sichuan Changhong Electric Co, recently told a group of foreign reporters.
"Some can survive and some can't survive," he said.
Changhong officials said the price war had cost the group millions of yuan in revenue and cut profit margins on individual televisions to 15-20 percent from 20-30 percent.
But, they said, competition was the new reality under China's market economy.
China's colour television producers manufacture around 50 million sets annually, against current demand of 15 million, Yu said.

The official Business News said on Tuesday that China's 1.2 billion people own 140 million colour television sets, with 93.5 sets for every 100 urban families and 22.9 sets for every 100 rural families. Investment in the television industry since the late 1970s had topped 25 billion yuan ($3 billion), the newspaper said.
Yu predicted some companies could be forced to shut down as there were just too many players in the market.
"In the end, China will have only a few brands," Yu said. "It won't be like now with tens of brands."
Changhong would continue to be number one, followed by Shenzhen-listed Konka Group Co Ltd, he said.
Third place would probably be a toss-up between Hong Kong-listed Nanjing Panda Electronics Co and Huizhou TCL Communications Equipment Co, which lists A shares in Shenzhen, Yu said.
In 1996, Changhong produced 4.8 million television sets, compared with 2.5 million for its nearest competitor Konka, Yu said.
Changhong weathered the price war by increasing production and grabbing more market share, which helped push profits to 2.5 billion yuan ($301.6 million) in 1996 against 1.8 billion in 1995, Yu said.
The listed subsidiary's net profit rose around 46 percent to 1.67 billion yuan in 1996 compared with 1995 on total turnover of 10.59 billion yuan, Changhong said.
For the future, Changhong aimed to focus on production of 25-inch (64 cm) and 29-inch (74 cm) models to meet demand for bigger screens, Yu said.
China's 1.2 billion people own 140 million colour television sets with 93.5 sets for every 100 urban families and 22.9 sets for every 100 rural families, official media has said.
Analysts said the major threat to Changhong came form foreign companies that had entered the Chinese television market, including Philips Electronics NV of the Netherlands and Japan's Sony Corp.

Although foreign companies command more advanced technology, Chinese consumers could be tempted by Changhong's cheaper prices, better service network and easier availability of spare parts, they said.

Changhong already exports a small number of its televisions to Southeast Asia, but the group would first learn to tussle with foreign companies on its own domestic turf before turning to large volume sales overseas, Yu said.
